headline: HESTA CIO emphasises portfolio diversification and deep scenario analysis as key defences against rising global macro volatility
reasoning: Sawtell-Rickson notes that volatility is inherent to investment markets and that sources of risk are very broad-based, spanning geopolitical conflict, climate events, AI disruption, and cyber threats. The primary response is portfolio diversification across assets, sectors, and regions, ensuring resilience to idiosyncratic risks. The team conducts stress tests and scenario analysis on potential market events to position the portfolio to benefit from positive thematics while hedging against tail risks. She also cautions against overreacting to short-term volatility, as doing so can erode long-term value creation.
quote: What do we do about that? (As an investor) we get rewarded for taking risk, but we want to make sure that we're taking risk - as much as we can - in the right areas. I think the first area that we focus on is diversification, to make sure our portfolio is diversified by assets, by sector, by region. We think deeply about how assets behave in different environments and alongside each other to make sure we are getting that diversification so the portfolio is resilient to specific, idiosyncratic risks. The second thing that we spend a lot of time on is deep research. We want to understand the current environment and regime, but also the potential future environments that we're facing into. We undertake stress tests on potential market events, and scenario analysis on potential paths forward. And we want to make sure that we're positioning the portfolio to benefit from the thematics that are coming that we think will be positive; and positioning it (the portfolio) against things that might be facing into risks, or tail events that we think could emerge. And it's the combination of those things that make a resilient portfolio. As long-term investors we also need to make sure that we're not overreacting to short-term volatility or risk, because really that can erode long-term value creation.

Where HESTA retains broader portfolio exposure to gambling companies, it engages with Australian gambling companies on harm minimisation. The fund also advocates to the Federal Government for a comprehensive national strategy, a national regulator, and a ban on online gambling advertising.
quote: The Sustainable Growth investment options also exclude any company that derives 5% or more revenue from the operation, licensing, and provision of key products or services fundamental to gambling operations. Our approach recognises that where engagement is possible, it is a preferable tool. Where we retain exposures, we use engagement and advocacy to seek to influence change, including on climate transition and gambling. We engage with Australian gambling companies on their approach to minimising harm, while also listening to our members and employers on how we can support the strengthening of regulation.

headline: HESTA has positioned its portfolio to capture AI-related upside where risk-adjusted returns are attractive, while maintaining broad diversification.
reasoning: HESTA describes AI as a key investment theme globally that is touching many sectors and assets. The fund has approached AI-aligned investments thoughtfully, seeking opportunities where pricing is supportive and risk-adjusted returns are attractive. The overall portfolio is designed to provide exposure to AI upside while maintaining diversifying assets. Members across various investment options may have indirect exposure to companies benefiting from AI growth.
quote: The US is the largest and most liquid investable market globally. It also likely has meaningful exposure to global growth as host to major AI companies. AI is a key investment theme globally, and HESTA has positioned the portfolio to take advantage where pricing is supportive. We have approached AI-aligned investments thoughtfully, seeking opportunities where risk-adjusted returns are attractive. HESTA's overall portfolio provides exposure to the potential upside from AI while maintaining a broad exposure to diversifying assets.

headline: HESTA CIO confirms exit of Israeli bank listings, state bonds, and weapons company holdings linked to Middle East conflict on heightened risk assessment
reasoning: HESTA's CIO Sonya Sawtell-Rickson confirmed the fund has been actively reducing its exposure to Israel-linked assets in response to geopolitical risks. The fund exited certain holdings in weapons companies associated with the conflict, exited listings on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange relating to Israeli banks, and exited some bond holdings for the State of Israel. The fund already maintains a portfolio-wide exclusion on controversial weapons (cluster munitions, anti-personnel mines, biological/chemical weapons) and nuclear weapons. Following these exits, direct regional exposure stands at less than 0.1% of the portfolio, described as very immaterial from a regional exposure and portfolio risk perspective. The fund continues to monitor the situation and retains some assets in the region including software and pharmaceutical companies.
quote: This is an area that we've been monitoring and focussed on and responding to for a while. It's worth reminding everybody we do have an exclusion in the portfolio around controversial weapons and also nuclear weapons. So that's a portfolio wide exclusion that is in place. But in addition, given the nature of this conflict and the risks that we're facing into, we've also exited certain holdings in weapons companies associated with the conflict. We've exited certain listings on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange relating to Israeli banks. And we've also exited some bond holdings for the state of Israel. Standing here today, our holdings to the region, direct holdings, to the regions are about 0.1%, less than 0.1%. So very immaterial now from a from a regional exposure and a portfolio risk perspective. And we continue to monitor the issues.

headline: HESTA scaling internal investment management capability with nearly one in five member dollars now managed in-house as at end of FY2025
reasoning: The CEO noted that as at end of FY2025, nearly one in five member dollars was managed internally by HESTA teams, reflecting scaling up of internal investment management capability as a strategic priority. This internal capability build was identified as part of the Investment Committee's focus for the year alongside strengthening investment operations. The move toward internalisation is consistent with trends among large Australian superannuation funds seeking to reduce costs and improve alignment with long-term investment objectives.
quote: The CEO advised that as at the end of FY2025, nearly one in five member dollars was managed internally by HESTA teams, reflecting collaboration across the Board, management and external partners. The CEO provided a brief update on investment strategy, noting that the Investment Committee's focus during the year included scaling up of internal investment management capability, strengthening investment operations and supporting strategic priorities.

headline: HESTA notes RBA hiked rates 0.25% in February with three of four big banks predicting a hold for 2026, with NAB the outlier forecasting one more rise.
reasoning: HESTA relayed that three of the big four Australian banks are predicting a hold on interest rates for 2026 following the RBA's 0.25% rate hike on 4 February, while NAB is forecasting one additional rate rise in 2026. HESTA itself declined to comment on the likelihood of further moves, focusing instead on its commitment to delivering long-term returns for members.
quote: If you're asking about Australia's central bank interest rates, HESTA cannot comment on the likelihood of an increase. However, three of the big four banks predict a hold on rates for 2026 after the RBA hiked rates by 0.25% on 4 February, with NAB predicting one more rate rise in 2026.

headline: HESTA maintains portfolio-wide exclusion on companies deriving 15%+ revenue from thermal coal mining
reasoning: HESTA applies a portfolio-wide exclusion to any company deriving 15% or more of its revenue from the mining of thermal coal. For members wanting broader exclusions, the Sustainable Growth option excludes any revenue from thermal coal mining or exploration, oil and gas extraction, production or refining, as well as companies with proved and probable thermal coal or metallurgical coal reserves. The fund prefers engagement over divestment where possible, and actively engages with large emitters on climate transition aligned with the Paris Agreement.
quote: HESTA has portfolio wide exclusions in place relating to any company that derives 15% or more revenue from the mining of thermal coal. For members that want an investment option that applies a broader range of investment exclusions aligned with their social and environmental values, we offer the Sustainable Growth investment option for both accumulation and income stream. The Sustainable Growth investment options exclude investment in any company that derives any revenue from the mining or exploration of thermal coal; any revenue from the extraction, production, refining of conventional and unconventional oil and gas; has any total volume proved and probable reserves of thermal coal and metallurgical coal; or, has any total volume of proved reserves of oil and gas.

headline: HESTA research finds eligible retirees missed $2.46 billion in retirement benefits in 2024-25 by not transitioning to retirement phase
reasoning: HESTA commissioned Laneway Analytics to study the behaviour of members eligible to move from accumulation to income stream phase. Research found that Australians who delayed the transition missed out on up to $2.46 billion in retirement benefits in 2024-25, primarily because retirement phase offers tax-free investment earnings. Members cited complexity, health issues, divorce and redundancy as reasons for delay. Currently, funds are legally restricted from actively guiding members into specific retirement products.
quote: HESTA commissioned Laneway Analytics to undertake research on retirees who do not move from accumulation phase to income stream when they are eligible. The research highlighted that Australians who are eligible to move into retirement phase missed out on up to $2.46 billion in 2024-25 in retirement benefits by not transitioning their superannuation to retirement phase, where they could benefit from tax-free investment earnings. Currently, funds are not able to actively guide members into specific retirement products, and our research shows the cost to members of funds not being able to do this.

headline: HESTA monitors geopolitical risks and exited Israeli bank and bond holdings on risk assessment grounds
reasoning: HESTA exited holdings in several banks listed on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange and bonds issued by the State of Israel, citing higher risk following an assessment of geopolitical conditions. The fund frames this as a fiduciary decision to protect member returns rather than an ethical divestment per se. The change is to be formally reflected in December 2025 holdings, due for release in March 2026. The fund states it continues to closely monitor geopolitical events and their potential financial materiality to the portfolio.
quote: Last year we exited holdings in several banks listed on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange and bonds issued by the State of Israel. This decision was made to protect member returns following an assessment of higher risk. This change will be formally reflected in the December 2025 holdings, due to be released in March 2026.

headline: HESTA CIO highlights $6.4bn invested in climate solutions and remains committed to renewable energy and green technology as attractive risk-adjusted return opportunities aligned with 2030 climate targets
reasoning: The CIO confirmed HESTA is on track to achieve its 2030 climate targets, with $6.4 billion invested in climate solutions such as renewable energy, sustainable property and other green technologies as at 30 June 2025. The CIO framed these investments as offering attractive risk-adjusted returns while generating real-world impact. The CEO also emphasised expected opportunities from Australia's transition to a lower-carbon economy and HESTA's scale and long-term investment horizon as advantages in capturing these opportunities.
quote: The CIO advised that HESTA remains focused on delivering strong investment performance while generating real-world impact and advised that HESTA is on track to achieve its 2030 climate targets. The CIO noted that through investments in renewable energy and storage, sustainable property and other green technologies, HESTA continues to invest in opportunities offering attractive risk-adjusted returns aligned with these targets. As at 30 June 2025, HESTA had $6.4 billion invested in climate solutions such as renewable energy and sustainable property.

headline: HESTA CIO sees AI as major investment opportunity across three segments: direct equity, infrastructure, and stewardship engagement
reasoning: Sonya Sawtell-Rickson frames AI across three investment dimensions. First, as a direct equity opportunity — companies linked to AI have been performing strongly, with growing profit margins and rising adoption driving returns. Second, as an infrastructure opportunity — AI adoption is creating demand for data centres and energy provision. Third, as a risk management and stewardship challenge — AI is a disruptive technology with winners and losers, and HESTA has initiated an engagement program with companies on responsible AI use, governance, and cyber risk transparency.
quote: The way we think about AI is across three segments. Firstly, as an investment opportunity. We know companies linked to AI have been performing incredibly strongly and that thematic has been paying off. The growth has been strong and profit margins are growing as we're seeing more adoption and demand emerging. This is creating other investment opportunities in areas such as data centres and the provision of energy to support the AI adoption. We're spending a lot of time on the investment opportunity element of it. The other side of that argument though is risk; it's a disruptive technology. There will be winners and losers coming out from AI and it will impact industries. We want to make sure that we're underwriting that transition effectively and proactively positioning the portfolio, so we don't have any undue risk exposures to the transition.

headline: HESTA CIO signals further internalisation of investment management is under exploration but no new asset classes decided yet
reasoning: Sonya Sawtell-Rickson indicated that having established internal capability in Australian Equities, Fixed Interest and Cash, HESTA is now working with the Board to explore what further asset classes or strategies could be managed in-house. The key criteria are whether HESTA can build a comparative advantage and whether internalisation would deliver net performance benefits to members. She emphasised this remains exploratory with nothing decided, but it forms part of the fund's strategic roadmap.
quote: As we look forward, I think the thing we're now turning our minds to is, what next? We're working with the Board to explore potential opportunities, staying very focused on making sure that we think we can build a comparative advantage and make sure that we can deliver those net performance benefits to our members. At this stage, nothing's been decided, but I think it will continue to be part of the sort of strategic roadmap of exploration as we go forward.

headline: HESTA CIO outlines internalisation strategy, growing in-house management from ~10% to 18% of portfolio by June 2025
reasoning: Sonya Sawtell-Rickson described HESTA's internalisation journey, which began with Australian Equities and expanded into Australian Fixed Interest, Cash and Term Deposits. By 30 June 2025, approximately 18% of the portfolio was managed in-house, up from just over 10% a year prior. The rationale for internalisation includes improved capability, more direct market access, new investment insights, access to new opportunities, and ultimately driving net investment performance at lower cost. She noted the board is actively exploring what asset classes or capabilities to internalise next, though no decisions have been made.
quote: We embarked on our internalisation journey a few years ago. And really our ambition was to try and deliver benefits for our members. These benefits were everything from improved capability, having more direct access to markets with new insights to feed into our investment process, and access to new opportunities as we were operating at different levels in markets. Ultimately, all of this is about driving net investment performance for our members, at a lower cost. So that was our ambition. We started with Australian Equities and then expanded into Australian Fixed Interest and Cash and Term Deposits. So as at the end of last financial year, 30 June 2025, we ran about 18% of the portfolio in-house, up from just over 10% a year prior.
